# Framework Development and Results {#sec-chapter4}

This chapter presents the construction and application of the TOPSIS-based prioritisation framework. It covers data preparation, indicator normalisation and weight assignment, TOPSIS computation, and the interpretation of results. The sensitivity analysis, which constitutes an evaluation activity, is presented in @sec-chapter5. The complete Python implementation used to produce all outputs in this chapter is provided as a reproducible artefact in Appendix A.

## Data Preparation {#sec-dataprep}

The dataset covers five IT services drawn from the trading IT division of the case organisation, extracted from its ITSM instance. Services were included on two criteria: they must be registered as active configuration items and must have a minimum operational history of six months within the twelve-month observation window, sufficient to produce stable indicator estimates. Services with fewer than three recorded production changes during the window were assigned the portfolio mean for CFR, consistent with the imputation approach recommended for sparse operational datasets [@grecoMethodologicalFrameworkComposite2019]. All service identifiers were replaced with alphanumeric codes prior to analysis, as described in Section 3.2.1. No team, vendor or individual identifiers are present in the dataset.

The five indicators are operationally defined as follows, consistent with the definitions established in Section 3.1.4. Incident frequency is the total number of P2 and P3 incidents attributed to the service during the observation window, divided by service age in months. MTTR is the arithmetic mean of elapsed hours between incident creation and resolution across all P2 and P3 incidents within the window. CFR is the proportion of production changes that resulted in an unplanned rollback or a subsequent incident within 72 hours of deployment. Patch currency is the proportion of components in the service's CMDB dependency stack whose installed version falls within a currently supported release window.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SVC-01 | 1.8| 38.4 | 0.27 | 0.52 | 0.52 |
| SVC-02 | 0.9| 15.2 | 0.12 | 0.75 | 0.75 |
| SVC-03 | 2.4| 47.1 | 0.33 | 0.46 | 0.46 |
| SVC-04 | 0.3| 5.8  | 0.03 | 0.94 | 0.94 |
| SVC-05 | 0.4| 44.2 | 0.05 | 0.89 | 0.89 |

Incident frequency, MTTR and CFR are cost criteria, for which lower values indicate lower technical debt severity. Patch currency is a benefit criterion, for which higher values are preferable.

### Data Limitations

As established in @sec-transfer, the operational data used here carry inherent quality limitations that must be explicitly acknowledged. Incident P2/P3 classifications vary across teams, reflecting local triage conventions rather than a uniform severity standard. CFR captures documentation practices as much as technical outcomes, since change records depend on consistent logging discipline. Patch recency is bounded by CMDB coverage and scanner configuration, meaning services with incomplete configuration records may appear more current than they are.

These limitations do not invalidate the proxy approach. To reduce their influence on the rankings, raw indicator values were inspected for implausible entries prior to normalisation, and services with materially incomplete CMDB records were flagged during data preparation (@sec-dataprep). No imputation was applied; missing values were treated as worst-case observations to avoid introducing artificial precision. Score precision is therefore constrained by data quality, and results should be interpreted as ordinal priority signals rather than exact measurements.

## Indicator Normalisation and Weighting

Before aggregation, each indicator is normalised using vector normalisation to remove differences in scale and unit:

$$r_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{m} x_{ij}^2}}$$

Vector normalisation is preferred over min-max normalisation because it preserves proportional relationships between values without compressing the range to a fixed interval, a property that @grecoMethodologicalFrameworkComposite2019 recommend for composite indicators where extreme values carry substantive meaning. A service with an unusually high MTTR should retain its full distance from lower-performing services in the normalised space rather than be pulled toward a truncated maximum. A weighted normalised matrix is then constructed by multiplying each normalised value by its criterion weight:

$$v_{ij} = w_j \cdot r_{ij}$$

Two weight configurations are applied. The baseline equal-weight configuration assigns $w_j = 0.20$ to each criterion and serves as the reference case against which the differential configuration is evaluated. The differential configuration assigns higher weights to MTTR and CFR.

This reflects a design judgement rather than a claim attributable to a single empirical source, and it is grounded in three converging observations from the literature. First, @ramasubbuManagingTechnicalDebt2015 establish that technical debt in COTS enterprise systems increases the probability of system failures by up to 62 percent, identifying incident frequency as the most directly observable TD signal in vendor-platform environments. This makes the speed of recovery from those incidents, captured by MTTR, the dimension most consequential to operational governance once a failure has occurred. Second, @nordExamplesTechnicalDebts2021 classify delivery tempo degradation and deployment instability explicitly as observable symptoms from which technical debt can be detected and prioritised in production environments. This provides direct grounding for elevating the weights of both MTTR and CFR relative to the remaining three criteria. Third, @fungprasertkulTechnicalDebtMonitoring2024 establish that TD dimensions can and should be assigned differential weights to reflect stakeholder perspectives and operational context. This provides methodological precedent for a two-configuration design: a baseline equal-weight case tested against a configuration calibrated to the trading IT domain.

Two weight configurations are applied, as specified in @sec-frameworkdesign. The baseline equal-weight configuration assigns $w_j = 0.20$ to each criterion and serves as the reference case. The differential configuration assigns higher weights to MTTR and CFR, reflecting their higher operational salience in a trading environment. Speed of recovery and deployment stability are the dimensions most directly consequential to financial exposure. This is a design judgement grounded in the literature synthesis in @sec-chapter2 rather than a single empirical claim. The differential weights are $w_{\text{MTTR}} = w_{\text{CFR}} = 0.30$ and $w_{\text{IncFreq}} = w_{\text{Patch}} = w_{\text{UnsupCompMon}} 0.133$.

| Configuration | Incident Freq. | MTTR | CFR | Patch Currency | Unsup. comp. months |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal (baseline) | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0.20 |
| Differential | 0.133 | 0.30 | 0.30 | 0.133 | 0.133 |

## TOPSIS Computation and Rankings

The TOPSIS procedure follows the formulation of [@hwangMultipleAttributeDecision1981]. After constructing the weighted normalised matrix, the positive and negative ideal solutions are identified:

$$A^{+} = \{v_1^{+}, \ldots, v_n^{+}\}, \quad A^{-} = \{v_1^{-}, \ldots, v_n^{-}\}$$

Where $v_j^{+}$ is the minimum weighted normalised value for cost criteria and the maximum for the benefit criterion, with $v_j^{-}$ being the converse. Euclidean distances from each ideal are computed for every service:

$$S_i^{+} = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n}(v_{ij} - v_j^{+})^2}, \quad S_i^{-} = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n}(v_{ij} - v_j^{-})^2}$$

The closeness coefficient constitutes the final priority score:

$$C_i = \frac{S_i^{-}}{S_i^{+} + S_i^{-}}, \quad C_i \in [0,1]$$

A higher $C_i$ indicates a service closer to the worst-case operational profile, representing a higher technical debt priority. The full results are presented in @tbl-topsis-results.

| Service | $S_i^{+}$ | $S_i^{-}$ | $C_i$ (equal) | Rank (equal) | $C_i$ (diff.) | Rank (diff.) |
|---------|-----------|-----------|--------------|-------------|--------------|-------------|
| SVC-04  | 0.0084 | 0.1982 | 0.9596 | 2  | 0.9616 | 2  |
| SVC-02  | 0.0644 | 0.1429 | 0.6893 | 5  | 0.6962 | 5  |
| SVC-05  | 0.1043 | 0.1574 | 0.6015 | 6  | 0.5633 | 7  |
| SVC-01  | 0.1622 | 0.0453 | 0.2183 | 11 | 0.2093 | 11 |
| SVC-03  | 0.2064 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 12 | 0.0000 | 12 |

: TOPSIS closeness coefficients and rankings, sorted by equal-weight rank. {#tbl-topsis-results}

Ten of the twelve services occupy the same rank position under both weight configurations. The only change occurs between SVC-05 and SVC-06, which swap at positions six and seven. SVC-05 presents a low incident frequency and a low CFR but a very high MTTR of 44.2 hours, suggesting that when failures occur, resolution is slow. This profile is consistent with infrastructure or dependency debt, where the root cause of incidents lies deep in the service stack rather than in surface-level code quality [@hakiDigitalNudging2023]. SVC-06 shows the inverse pattern: frequent failures and a higher CFR, but a very low MTTR of 7.1 hours, indicating deployment instability that is contained quickly. Under equal weights, the low incident frequency and CFR of SVC-05 outweigh its recovery penalty. When MTTR and CFR receive higher weights in the differential configuration, SVC-06's fast-recovery advantage is amplified and SVC-05's elevated MTTR is penalised more heavily. The overall Kendall's $\tau$ between the two configurations is 0.97, confirming that the single swap is the only substantive divergence.
